Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A Coin World analysis of U.S. Mint production data revealed that the total output of circulating coins from the Denver and Philadelphia Mints for the first five months of 2023 reached 6,110,660,000 units, a nearly 8% increase compared to the same period in 2022. [1] The report, published on June 11, 2023, detailed the production figures for Lincoln cents, Jefferson 5-cent coins, Roosevelt dimes, and American Women quarter dollars. [1] The analysis covered production through the end of May 2023. <2> The U.S. Supreme Court issued an 8-1 ruling on June 1, 2023, in the case of Glacier Northwest Inc. v. International Brotherhood of Teamsters, making it easier for companies to sue labor unions for damages to company property that occur during strikes. [2, 3, 4] The Court held that the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) does not shield unions from state lawsuits when members do not take "reasonable precautions" to avoid foreseeable damage to company property during a work stoppage. [2, 3, 5] The case stemmed from a 2017 dispute where concrete truck drivers went on strike, leading to the hardening and destruction of the concrete in their trucks. [8] Glacier Northwest sued, arguing the union timed the strike to intentionally destroy its property. [8, 9] In her dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson argued the ruling "risks erosion of the right to strike" and could create confusion about federally protected labor activities. [2] The decision is seen as a blow to organized labor, potentially increasing the legal and financial risks for unions engaging in strikes. [8] <3> Capstone Copper reported that its Pinto Valley mine in Arizona experienced a challenging first quarter in 2023 due to heavy rainfall and flooding. These weather events caused operational disruptions, including plugged chutes and screens, which resulted in lower mill throughput and a 10% decrease in production compared to the first quarter of 2022. Despite these setbacks, the company reaffirmed its consolidated production guidance for 2023, maintaining a target of 170-190 thousand tonnes of copper. Capstone anticipates that production will increase sequentially, with a corresponding decrease in costs, in the second half of 2023. <4> Jervois Global announced its decision to suspend the final construction and full concentrator commissioning at its Idaho Cobalt Operations (ICO), which was set to be the only primary cobalt mine in the United States. The Australian company cited low cobalt prices and inflationary pressures on construction costs as the primary reasons for the halt. The facility was also designed to produce copper and gold as by-products. Jervois stated its intention to complete construction and commission the plant when cobalt prices recover. The company had invested approximately US$130 million into the project's construction. <5> During a significant en banc hearing before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on March 21, 2023, in the case of Apache Stronghold v. United States, legal arguments were presented regarding the proposed Resolution Copper mine in Arizona. [1, 2, 5] A central issue in the ongoing legal dispute is the Apache people's claim that the destruction of the sacred site Oak Flat would violate their religious freedom, a right they argue is protected in part by an 1852 treaty with the U.S. government. [4, 6, 7] In opposition, the U.S. Forest Service has contended that this treaty does not grant the Apache rights to the land under which the massive copper deposit is located. This hearing was a key event in the legal battle to prevent the federal government from transferring the land to Resolution Copper, which would lead to the eventual collapse of Oak Flat as a result of the mining process. [1] News of the oral arguments and the positions taken by both sides was reported on the same day as the hearing. <6> The failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) on March 10, 2023, marked the third-largest bank failure in U.S. history and triggered a significant financial crisis. [3] On that day, the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation closed the bank and appointed the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) as receiver following a massive bank run where depositors attempted to withdraw $42 billion in a single day. [5, 7] The collapse sent shockwaves through the U.S. banking industry, leading to the subsequent failures of Signature Bank and First Republic Bank and prompting Moody's to downgrade its outlook for the entire U.S. banking system to negative. [6, 8, 12] In response, U.S. regulators, including the Treasury Department, Federal Reserve, and FDIC, took extraordinary measures to prevent systemic contagion by guaranteeing all deposits at SVB and Signature Bank and establishing a new Bank Term Funding Program to shore up liquidity for other institutions. [4, 7] The banking turmoil directly impacted commodity markets; by mid-March, copper prices fell as concerns about a potential global banking crisis and a stronger U.S. dollar weighed on the market. [9, 13, 17] While the banking crisis was a notable factor, copper prices in 2023 were also influenced by other significant economic forces, including weaker-than-expected demand from China, rising global interest rates, and supply disruptions. [19, 20] <7> On January 26, 2023, U.S. Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland signed Public Land Order 7917, enacting a 20-year ban on mining and geothermal leasing on approximately 225,504 acres of the Superior National Forest in northeastern Minnesota. [2, 3, 7] This order is intended to protect the Rainy River watershed, which includes the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and the 1854 Ceded Territory of the Chippewa Bands, from the potential negative impacts of new mining operations. [2, 7] The decision effectively halts the development of the proposed Twin Metals underground mine, a project by a subsidiary of Antofagasta PLC, which planned to extract copper, nickel, cobalt, and platinum group metals. [2, 10] The action followed a U.S. Forest Service proposal in 2021 and a comprehensive scientific review which concluded that sulfide-ore copper mining could cause irreversible pollution to the Boundary Waters. [7, 10] The order became effective on January 31, 2023. [4, 6]

metadata.original_text: This time series records copper USD Lbs data in the Commodity market price domain, with a collection frequency of daily, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2023-08-18 to 2023-09-04. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In June 2023, the U.S. Department of Labor's Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) conducted impact inspections at 18 mines across 12 states, resulting in the issuance of 242 violations. These targeted inspections are part of a program initiated after the 2010 Upper Big Branch mine explosion and focus on mines with a history of compliance issues, accidents, injuries, or other safety concerns. Among the 242 violations, 71 were categorized as "significant and substantial," and four were identified as "unwarrantable failure findings," which indicates aggravated conduct beyond ordinary negligence. The inspections took place in Alabama, Illinois, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wyoming. Assistant Secretary for Mine Safety and Health, Chris Williamson, expressed concern that these inspections continue to uncover hazards that are known root causes of fatal accidents and serious illnesses. <2> In a CME Group report published in July 2023, it was noted that COMEX copper first position experienced a price increase in the first half of June 2023, trading in the $3.70-$3.90 per pound range. This rise followed the resolution of the U.S. debt ceiling crisis, which concluded with the signing of the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 on June 3, 2023. However, after June 23, 2023, copper prices faced downward pressure. This was attributed to a strengthening U.S. dollar and the prospect of further interest rate hikes by central banks like the Fed, ECB, and Bank of England to control inflation. <3> A weekly market report for the U.S. Midwest, covering the period of June 16th to June 22nd, 2023, indicated a slight increase in copper scrap prices. Among the top gainers were Copper Radiators, #3 Copper-Light Copper, and #2 Copper Wire and Tubing. Specifically, the prices for #3 Copper-Light Copper and #2 Copper Wire and Tubing rose to $3.48 per pound and $3.58 per pound, respectively, by the end of the period. <4> Rio Tinto announced its approval of $498 million in funding for the underground development and infrastructure of the North Rim Skarn (NRS) area at its Kennecott copper mine near Salt Lake City, Utah. [2, 5] This investment aims to bolster the U.S. copper supply to meet increasing demand for domestic manufacturing and the energy transition. [2, 3] Production from the NRS is scheduled to commence in 2024, with an expected ramp-up period of two years. [5, 6] The project is anticipated to yield approximately 250,000 tonnes of additional mined copper over the subsequent ten years, supplementing the output from open-cut operations. [2, 5, 6] This funding is part of a larger investment in the Kennecott operation, which also includes a $300 million rebuild of the smelter and a $120 million upgrade to the refinery and molybdenum flotation circuit. [6, 7] <5> A Coin World analysis of U.S. Mint production data revealed that the total output of circulating coins from the Denver and Philadelphia Mints for the first five months of 2023 reached 6,110,660,000 units, a nearly 8% increase compared to the same period in 2022. [1] The report, published on June 11, 2023, detailed the production figures for Lincoln cents, Jefferson 5-cent coins, Roosevelt dimes, and American Women quarter dollars. [1] The analysis covered production through the end of May 2023. <6> The U.S. Supreme Court issued an 8-1 ruling on June 1, 2023, in the case of Glacier Northwest Inc. v. International Brotherhood of Teamsters, making it easier for companies to sue labor unions for damages to company property that occur during strikes. [2, 3, 4] The Court held that the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) does not shield unions from state lawsuits when members do not take "reasonable precautions" to avoid foreseeable damage to company property during a work stoppage. [2, 3, 5] The case stemmed from a 2017 dispute where concrete truck drivers went on strike, leading to the hardening and destruction of the concrete in their trucks. [8] Glacier Northwest sued, arguing the union timed the strike to intentionally destroy its property. [8, 9] In her dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson argued the ruling "risks erosion of the right to strike" and could create confusion about federally protected labor activities. [2] The decision is seen as a blow to organized labor, potentially increasing the legal and financial risks for unions engaging in strikes. [8] <7> Capstone Copper reported that its Pinto Valley mine in Arizona experienced a challenging first quarter in 2023 due to heavy rainfall and flooding. These weather events caused operational disruptions, including plugged chutes and screens, which resulted in lower mill throughput and a 10% decrease in production compared to the first quarter of 2022. Despite these setbacks, the company reaffirmed its consolidated production guidance for 2023, maintaining a target of 170-190 thousand tonnes of copper. Capstone anticipates that production will increase sequentially, with a corresponding decrease in costs, in the second half of 2023. <8> Jervois Global announced its decision to suspend the final construction and full concentrator commissioning at its Idaho Cobalt Operations (ICO), which was set to be the only primary cobalt mine in the United States. The Australian company cited low cobalt prices and inflationary pressures on construction costs as the primary reasons for the halt. The facility was also designed to produce copper and gold as by-products. Jervois stated its intention to complete construction and commission the plant when cobalt prices recover. The company had invested approximately US$130 million into the project's construction. <9> During a significant en banc hearing before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on March 21, 2023, in the case of Apache Stronghold v. United States, legal arguments were presented regarding the proposed Resolution Copper mine in Arizona. [1, 2, 5] A central issue in the ongoing legal dispute is the Apache people's claim that the destruction of the sacred site Oak Flat would violate their religious freedom, a right they argue is protected in part by an 1852 treaty with the U.S. government. [4, 6, 7] In opposition, the U.S. Forest Service has contended that this treaty does not grant the Apache rights to the land under which the massive copper deposit is located. This hearing was a key event in the legal battle to prevent the federal government from transferring the land to Resolution Copper, which would lead to the eventual collapse of Oak Flat as a result of the mining process. [1] News of the oral arguments and the positions taken by both sides was reported on the same day as the hearing. <10> The failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) on March 10, 2023, marked the third-largest bank failure in U.S. history and triggered a significant financial crisis. [3] On that day, the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation closed the bank and appointed the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) as receiver following a massive bank run where depositors attempted to withdraw $42 billion in a single day. [5, 7] The collapse sent shockwaves through the U.S. banking industry, leading to the subsequent failures of Signature Bank and First Republic Bank and prompting Moody's to downgrade its outlook for the entire U.S. banking system to negative. [6, 8, 12] In response, U.S. regulators, including the Treasury Department, Federal Reserve, and FDIC, took extraordinary measures to prevent systemic contagion by guaranteeing all deposits at SVB and Signature Bank and establishing a new Bank Term Funding Program to shore up liquidity for other institutions. [4, 7] The banking turmoil directly impacted commodity markets; by mid-March, copper prices fell as concerns about a potential global banking crisis and a stronger U.S. dollar weighed on the market. [9, 13, 17] While the banking crisis was a notable factor, copper prices in 2023 were also influenced by other significant economic forces, including weaker-than-expected demand from China, rising global interest rates, and supply disruptions. [19, 20]

The country's ongoing property crisis exerted downward pressure on copper prices throughout much of 2023, disrupting typical seasonal demand patterns, as seen in September when demand fell during a period it usually rises. This broader trend was also reflected in a reported 11.7% year-on-year decrease in profits for China's industrial enterprises from January to July. <3> Following a meeting in Lisbon, Portugal, on October 3-4, 2023, the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) forecast a global refined copper supply surplus of 467,000 metric tons for 2024. [2] The improved outlook was attributed to the startup or expansion of smelters and refineries, with higher production anticipated from the sustained expansion of China's electrolytic capacity and new or expanded facilities in India, Indonesia, and the United States. [2] <4> In early October 2023, copper prices experienced a significant decline, influenced by a combination of macroeconomic factors. A primary driver was the strengthening of the U.S. dollar, supported by high interest rates, which made the dollar-denominated metal more expensive for buyers using other currencies. Concurrently, there was a notable increase in copper inventories in London Metal Exchange (LME)-registered warehouses, signaling ample supply. Additional pressures included concerns over weaker demand from China, a major consumer, due to its ongoing real estate crisis and a slow post-pandemic economic rebound. Among the 242 violations, 71 were categorized as "significant and substantial," and four were identified as "unwarrantable failure findings," which indicates aggravated conduct beyond ordinary negligence. The inspections took place in Alabama, Illinois, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wyoming. [2, 5] This investment aims to bolster the U.S. copper supply to meet increasing demand for domestic manufacturing and the energy transition. [2, 5, 6] This funding is part of a larger investment in the Kennecott operation, which also includes a $300 million rebuild of the smelter and a $120 million upgrade to the refinery and molybdenum flotation circuit. [1] The report, published on June 11, 2023, detailed the production figures for Lincoln cents, Jefferson 5-cent coins, Roosevelt dimes, and American Women quarter dollars. [1] The analysis covered production through the end of May 2023. <10> The U.S. Supreme Court issued an 8-1 ruling on June 1, 2023, in the case of Glacier Northwest Inc. v. International Brotherhood of Teamsters, making it easier for companies to sue labor unions for damages to company property that occur during strikes. [2, 3, 4] The Court held that the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) does not shield unions from state lawsuits when members do not take "reasonable precautions" to avoid foreseeable damage to company property during a work stoppage. [2, 3, 5] The case stemmed from a 2017 dispute where concrete truck drivers went on strike, leading to the hardening and destruction of the concrete in their trucks. [8] Glacier Northwest sued, arguing the union timed the strike to intentionally destroy its property. [8, 9] In her dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson argued the ruling "risks erosion of the right to strike" and could create confusion about federally protected labor activities. [2] The decision is seen as a blow to organized labor, potentially increasing the legal and financial risks for unions engaging in strikes. [8]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 23, 2023, copper prices rebounded after hitting an 11-month low.; The earlier price drop was attributed to concerns over the Middle East conflict and weaker demand from China.; The rebound saw the price for November delivery rise on the Comex market in New York. <2> On October 23, 2023, the price of copper on the London Metal Exchange fell to an 11-month low of US$7,856 per tonne, equivalent to approximately US$3.56 per pound. This significant price drop was primarily attributed to reduced demand from China's struggling real estate sector. The country's ongoing property crisis exerted downward pressure on copper prices throughout much of 2023, disrupting typical seasonal demand patterns, as seen in September when demand fell during a period it usually rises. This broader trend was also reflected in a reported 11.7% year-on-year decrease in profits for China's industrial enterprises from January to July. While prices rebounded slightly after the October low, the year was characterized by this sustained pressure, . <3> Following a meeting in Lisbon, Portugal, on October 3-4, 2023, the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) forecast a global refined copper supply surplus of 467,000 metric tons for 2024. [2] This represented a significant shift from an estimated deficit of 27,000 metric tons in 2023. [2] The improved outlook was attributed to the startup or expansion of smelters and refineries, with higher production anticipated from the sustained expansion of China's electrolytic capacity and new or expanded facilities in India, Indonesia, and the United States. [2] <4> In early October 2023, copper prices experienced a significant decline, influenced by a combination of macroeconomic factors. A primary driver was the strengthening of the U.S. dollar, supported by high interest rates, which made the dollar-denominated metal more expensive for buyers using other currencies. Concurrently, there was a notable increase in copper inventories in London Metal Exchange (LME)-registered warehouses, signaling ample supply. Additional pressures included concerns over weaker demand from China, a major consumer, due to its ongoing real estate crisis and a slow post-pandemic economic rebound. By October 23, 2023, copper prices on the LME had fallen to $7,856 a tonne, their lowest point in 11 months, before seeing a slight rebound. <5> In June 2023, the U.S. Department of Labor's Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) conducted impact inspections at 18 mines across 12 states, resulting in the issuance of 242 violations. These targeted inspections are part of a program initiated after the 2010 Upper Big Branch mine explosion and focus on mines with a history of compliance issues, accidents, injuries, or other safety concerns. Among the 242 violations, 71 were categorized as "significant and substantial," and four were identified as "unwarrantable failure findings," which indicates aggravated conduct beyond ordinary negligence. The inspections took place in Alabama, Illinois, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wyoming. Assistant Secretary for Mine Safety and Health, Chris Williamson, expressed concern that these inspections continue to uncover hazards that are known root causes of fatal accidents and serious illnesses. <6> In a CME Group report published in July 2023, it was noted that COMEX copper first position experienced a price increase in the first half of June 2023, trading in the $3.70-$3.90 per pound range. This rise followed the resolution of the U.S. debt ceiling crisis, which concluded with the signing of the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 on June 3, 2023. However, after June 23, 2023, copper prices faced downward pressure. This was attributed to a strengthening U.S. dollar and the prospect of further interest rate hikes by central banks like the Fed, ECB, and Bank of England to control inflation. <7> A weekly market report for the U.S. Midwest, covering the period of June 16th to June 22nd, 2023, indicated a slight increase in copper scrap prices. Among the top gainers were Copper Radiators, #3 Copper-Light Copper, and #2 Copper Wire and Tubing. Specifically, the prices for #3 Copper-Light Copper and #2 Copper Wire and Tubing rose to $3.48 per pound and $3.58 per pound, respectively, by the end of the period. <8> Rio Tinto announced its approval of $498 million in funding for the underground development and infrastructure of the North Rim Skarn (NRS) area at its Kennecott copper mine near Salt Lake City, Utah. [2, 5] This investment aims to bolster the U.S. copper supply to meet increasing demand for domestic manufacturing and the energy transition. [2, 3] Production from the NRS is scheduled to commence in 2024, with an expected ramp-up period of two years. [5, 6] The project is anticipated to yield approximately 250,000 tonnes of additional mined copper over the subsequent ten years, supplementing the output from open-cut operations. [2, 5, 6] This funding is part of a larger investment in the Kennecott operation, which also includes a $300 million rebuild of the smelter and a $120 million upgrade to the refinery and molybdenum flotation circuit. [6, 7] <9> A Coin World analysis of U.S. Mint production data revealed that the total output of circulating coins from the Denver and Philadelphia Mints for the first five months of 2023 reached 6,110,660,000 units, a nearly 8% increase compared to the same period in 2022. [1] The report, published on June 11, 2023, detailed the production figures for Lincoln cents, Jefferson 5-cent coins, Roosevelt dimes, and American Women quarter dollars. [1] The analysis covered production through the end of May 2023. <10> The U.S. Supreme Court issued an 8-1 ruling on June 1, 2023, in the case of Glacier Northwest Inc. v. International Brotherhood of Teamsters, making it easier for companies to sue labor unions for damages to company property that occur during strikes. [2, 3, 4] The Court held that the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) does not shield unions from state lawsuits when members do not take "reasonable precautions" to avoid foreseeable damage to company property during a work stoppage. [2, 3, 5] The case stemmed from a 2017 dispute where concrete truck drivers went on strike, leading to the hardening and destruction of the concrete in their trucks. [8] Glacier Northwest sued, arguing the union timed the strike to intentionally destroy its property. [8, 9] In her dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson argued the ruling "risks erosion of the right to strike" and could create confusion about federally protected labor activities. [2] The decision is seen as a blow to organized labor, potentially increasing the legal and financial risks for unions engaging in strikes. [8]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Capstone Copper Corp., an Americas-focused copper mining company headquartered in Vancouver, Canada, which owns and operates the Pinto Valley copper mine in Arizona, announced its schedule for releasing its second-quarter 2024 financial results. These routine corporate disclosures are significant for market analysis, providing insight into the performance of key industry players. <2> Copper prices on the Comex market reached a new all-time high of $5.20 per pound on May 20, 2024; The price was driven by expectations of Federal Reserve interest rate cuts; The price was driven by a tightening supply market <3> A report published in June 2024 highlighted bullish long-term forecasts for copper; This outlook is based on looming supply deficits; and surging demand from the global energy transition <4> In early June 2024, copper prices experienced a significant drop; falling over 2% to below $10,000 per metric ton.; This decline was attributed to a buildup in global inventories <5> A report in April 2024 highlighted a significant decrease in global copper smelting capacity during the first quarter of 2024.; The data, from geospatial intelligence firm Earth-i, showed that an average of 12.5% of global smelter capacity was inactive, a notable increase from 9.3% in the same period of 2023.; This reduction in processing capacity contributed to a tighter supply market. <6> A significant increase in copper demand is anticipated, driven by the burgeoning green energy sector. Copper is an essential component in renewable energy infrastructure and electric vehicles (EVs), with its demand in clean energy projected to comprise a substantial portion of the market in the coming years. This surge is due to green technologies using significantly more copper than their conventional counterparts. For instance, an electric vehicle requires approximately 2.4 times more copper, at 53 kilograms, than a traditional internal combustion engine car. [1] Similarly, renewable power sources like solar and wind infrastructure demand 2.5 to 7 times more copper than fossil fuel-based technologies. [1] Projections indicate that upgrades to the global electric grid could necessitate 427 million metric tons of copper by 2050, while EV-related demand alone is expected to reach 2.8 million metric tons by 2030. This growing imbalance between supply and demand fosters a long-term bullish outlook for copper prices, positioning copper miners to potentially benefit. <7> In the USA Midwest, prices for most grades of scrap copper increased during the week of January 12th to 18th, 2024. The price for #1 Copper Wire and Tubing concluded the week at $3.53 per pound, #2 Copper Wire and Tubing at $3.43 per pound, and #3 Copper-Light Copper at $3.33 per pound. [1] Conversely, Copper Radiators experienced a slight decline of 0.45% compared to the previous week. [1] <8> In its 2023 Critical Materials Assessment, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) officially added copper to its list of critical materials, a move seen as a positive development for the domestic industry. The determination, effective July 28, 2023, classified copper as "near-critical" in the medium term (2025-2035) due to its essential role in clean energy technologies and the growing risk of supply chain disruptions. This was the first time a U.S. government agency had included copper on an official critical materials list. The designation makes copper-related projects eligible for tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act. However, industry analysis noted that for a more substantial streamlining of the lengthy permitting process for new mining operations, copper would also need to be added to the separate critical minerals list compiled by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). <9> In early 2023, copper prices experienced significant volatility. Prices peaked in January, driven by optimism following the lifting of COVID-19 restrictions in China. [4] The COMEX futures contract reached a high of $4.3145 per pound, while London Metal Exchange (LME) prices hit a year-to-date high of $9,550.50 per tonne during the month. [4, 6] Supply concerns, including protests at mines in Peru, the world's second-largest copper producer, also contributed to the price rally. [6] However, this peak was followed by a downward trend as the initial optimism faded. [4] The lackluster economic recovery in China, particularly within its property sector, weighed on demand. [4] Furthermore, prices faced pressure throughout the year from a strengthening U.S. dollar, which makes commodities more expensive for importers, rising borrowing costs in developed economies, and broader fears of a global recession. [2, 4] <10> Following a unanimous ruling by Panama's Supreme Court on November 28, 2023, which declared the contract for the Cobre Panama copper mine unconstitutional, the Panamanian government ordered Canadian company First Quantum Minerals to cease operations. [3, 6, 8] President Laurentino Cortizo announced the commencement of the "orderly and safe closure of the mine" on the same day as the court's decision. [11] The Cobre Panama mine, operated by First Quantum's local subsidiary Minera Panamá, is a significant contributor to the nation's economy, accounting for approximately 5% of its GDP and 75% of its exports. [2, 11] The closure of the mine, which produces about 1.5% of the world's copper supply, has had a notable impact on the global copper market and contributed to price volatility.
